causalMechanism.primaryVector: Chronic elevated blood pressure damages the retinal microvasculature in a stereotyped sequence. The retinal arterioles first respond to pressure elevation with autoregulatory vasoconstriction, producing generalized and focal arteriolar narrowing; sustained hypertension then drives arteriolosclerosis — intimal thickening, medial hyperplasia, and hyaline degeneration — visible as arteriovenous nicking and altered vessel light reflexes; with further pressure elevation and endothelial dysfunction the blood-retinal barrier fails, producing flame and dot-blot hemorrhages, microaneurysms, cotton-wool spots, and hard exudates; and in accelerated or malignant hypertension, optic disc and macular edema develop. Because the retinal circulation is a directly visible microvascular bed, these changes track the severity and duration of blood pressure elevation, correlate with other end-organ damage such as left ventricular hypertrophy and renal impairment, and predict stroke and cardiovascular events — and blood pressure control prevents their progression. The clinical evidence is substantial: the Bhaktapur Retina population-based study of 643 elderly subjects with hypertension found hypertensive retinopathy in 12.6% (more frequent in diabetics at 16.49% and in those with body-mass index at or above 25); the classic review of how hypertension affects the eye documents the full spectrum of signs (generalized and focal arteriolar narrowing, arteriovenous nicking, hemorrhages, microaneurysms, and optic disc and macular edema in severe cases) and notes that mild hypertensive retinopathy signs appear in nearly 10% of the general adult non-diabetic population and associate with left ventricular hypertrophy and renal impairment; and the Nature Reviews Disease Primers review of hypertensive eye disease establishes the current clinical-standard framework for the spectrum and its systemic significance. Under 38 CFR § 3.310(a), hypertensive retinopathy developing in a veteran with service-connected hypertension is a direct-causation secondary claim. For an 'at least as likely as not' opinion, document serial blood pressure readings (the schedule requires values confirmed by readings taken two or more times on at least three different days), the fundoscopic findings with their severity or grading, and any visual impairment with acuity and field testing; and exclude competing causes — diabetic retinopathy (which has its own dedicated code and commonly coexists, so the presence of diabetes must be documented and its contribution weighed), retinal vein occlusion, hematologic disorders and coagulopathies, and other retinopathies. Where pre-existing retinopathy or a separate established retinal disease is documented before the hypertension, § 3.310(b) limits service connection to the attributable aggravation.

causalMechanism.primaryVector: Thiazide and loop diuretics raise serum uric acid and precipitate gout through a renal transport mechanism: volume depletion and reduced tubular flow increase proximal tubular urate reabsorption (net urate retention), and the resulting hyperuricemia is the direct precursor of gout — when serum urate exceeds its solubility, monosodium urate crystals deposit in joints and periarticular tissues and trigger the intense interleukin-1-driven inflammatory response of an acute gout flare, with recurrent attacks producing chronic gouty arthropathy and tophi. The effect is drug-class-specific (potassium-sparing diuretics do not show it), dose- and duration-related, persists during therapy, and is mediated by the change in serum urate — a mechanism confirmed by the observation that adjusting for urate level eliminates the association. The quantitative evidence is strong: a population-based case-control study of 91,530 incident gout cases and matched controls found adjusted odds ratios for current diuretic use of 2.64 (95% CI 2.47-2.83) for loop diuretics, 1.70 (95% CI 1.62-1.79) for thiazide diuretics, and 2.30 (95% CI 1.95-2.70) for thiazide-like diuretics, with combined loop and thiazide use carrying the highest risk (OR 4.65, 95% CI 3.51-6.16) and potassium-sparing agents showing no association (OR 1.06, 95% CI 0.91-1.23); the Atherosclerosis Risk in Communities cohort (5,789 adults with hypertension, 37% on diuretics) found any diuretic associated with incident gout (HR 1.48, 95% CI 1.11-1.98), with thiazide HR 1.44 (1.00-2.10) and loop HR 2.31 (1.36-3.91), a longitudinal serum urate increase of 0.72 mg/dL in those starting diuretics (P < 0.001), and the association becoming null after adjustment for urate — establishing mediation; and a population-based cohort of gout-naive hypertensive adults matched 4,045 to 4,045 found that thiazide initiation carried sustained higher risks of subsequently being prescribed antigout medication (adjusted hazard ratios 2.23, 2.07, and 2.41 for under 30 days, 31-180 days, and over 180 days). Under 38 CFR § 3.310(a), a disability proximately due to or resulting from the treatment of a service-connected condition is itself service-connected, so gout developing on documented chronic thiazide or loop diuretic therapy for service-connected hypertension is a treatment-complication secondary claim; where pre-existing gout or hyperuricemia is documented before diuretic exposure, § 3.310(b) limits service connection to the attributable aggravation. For an 'at least as likely as not' opinion, document the diuretic regimen (agent, dose, duration, dates, and any dose changes), serial serum urate values before and during therapy, the gout diagnosis (monosodium urate crystals on joint aspiration, or validated clinical/imaging criteria such as ultrasound double-contour sign or dual-energy CT), the joint distribution and attack frequency, and the chronology of attacks relative to diuretic initiation; and address competing causes — alcohol use (which has its own route to gout and must be documented), chronic kidney disease with impaired urate excretion, obesity and metabolic syndrome, purine-rich diet and fructose intake, family history, myeloproliferative and lymphoproliferative disorders, psoriasis, and other drugs such as low-dose aspirin and calcineurin inhibitors. Because no diagnostic code specifically addresses gout, the rating proceeds by analogy under § 4.20 to the § 4.71a joint-schedule entries.

causalMechanism.primaryVector: Hemodynamic wall-stress sequence: in service-connected hypertension, chronically elevated aortic wall tension and shear increase cyclic strain on an already age-degenerate media, promoting elastin fragmentation, collagen remodeling, matrix-metalloproteinase activation and smooth-muscle apoptosis; the resulting loss of tensile strength allows progressive dilatation. That mechanism superimposes on a pre-existing degenerative and atherosclerotic aortopathy, so the medically coherent theory is aggravation of a baseline process rather than creation of an aneurysm de novo. Kobeissi et al. (PMID 30903463), a systematic review and meta-analysis of cohort studies of blood pressure and abdominal aortic aneurysm, found that hypertension increased the risk of developing abdominal aortic aneurysm by about 66 percent, with a dose relationship across blood-pressure categories. Altobelli et al. (PMID 30544688), meta-analyzing population-based risk-factor studies, reported hypertension with an effect size of approximately 1.55 for abdominal aortic aneurysm alongside age, male sex and smoking. Takagi et al. (PMID 27521823) found hypertension positively associated with aneurysm presence but not with aneurysm expansion rate, which is an important internal counterweight: the literature supports an association with the existence of aneurysm disease while the evidence that hypertension drives growth of an already-measured aneurysm is weaker. These sources are observational, and smoking, age, male sex, family history and genetic syndromes are established competing drivers, so no individual probability follows from them.

These sources are observational, and smoking, age, male sex, family history and genetic syndromes are established competing drivers, so no individual probability follows from them.

Required individual evidence and competing causes: obtain the serial imaging record showing aneurysm dimensions, the rate of change and the site (ascending, thoracic, abdominal), contemporaneous blood-pressure records documenting chronic elevation and control, and the full vascular-risk profile. Cigarette smoking, advanced age, male sex, family history of aneurysm, connective-tissue disorders such as Marfan or Loeys-Dietz syndrome, bicuspid aortic valve, prior dissection, vasculitis and other atherosclerotic disease are competing causes that must be documented and apportioned; distinguishing a discrete fusiform aneurysm from aortic ectasia matters because the diagnostic code turns on measured diameter, symptoms and operative need. A temporal pattern in which elevated pressures predate documented dilatation, together with a measured increment beyond the expected age-related rate of change, favors the hypertensive-aggravation route; an aneurysm that is stable over years of documented hypertension, or that occurs in a heavy smoker with a strong family history, weakens the attribution to hypertension.

Legal and rating analysis: because the theory asserted here is aggravation, the governing provision is 38 CFR § 3.310(b), which requires a qualifying baseline (the pre-existing degenerative aortic wall condition, documented by earlier imaging or the natural history of the disease) and an attributable increase beyond the natural progression of that baseline; if the evidence instead supports the aneurysm as an outgrowth of the hypertension itself, the same facts may be analyzed as direct causation under § 3.310(a). An 'at least as likely as not' opinion requires the blood-pressure record, the imaging trajectory, and the competing causes — especially smoking — to be weighed so that the evidence is at least in approximate balance; population relative risks such as the 66 percent meta-analytic estimate describe groups and do not establish an individual probability. No individual probability is asserted here. Rating: § 4.104 DC 7110 provides a 100-percent evaluation only for an aneurysm that is 5 centimeters or larger, symptomatic, or requires surgery, and otherwise assigns 0 percent, so a small asymptomatic aneurysm is generally not compensable despite being service-connected secondary; DC 7101 governs the hypertension primary. Apply § 4.14 so that the same blood-pressure elevation and any cardiac or renal consequences are not rated twice, and note that § 4.104 directs that hypertension be evaluated separately from hypertensive heart disease. Landing this incoming route requires host-file review: the hypertension host identity is published and currently points to chronic kidney disease, ischemic heart disease, congestive heart failure and erectile dysfunction, and the aortic-aneurysm identity is draft with existing gout and tuberculosis inbound associations and outbound suggestions to valvular heart disease and hydronephrosis, so this hypertension route must be reconciled against that existing posture.

causalMechanism.primaryVector: Photosensitization and autoantibody-induction sequence: hydrochlorothiazide and its metabolites absorb ultraviolet radiation in the UVA range and, on photoactivation, generate reactive species that damage keratinocytes and alter the presentation of nuclear antigens; in genetically susceptible individuals this drives an interface dermatitis with prominent epidermal photosensitivity and induces Ro/SS-A (anti-SSA) autoantibodies directed against a ribonucleoprotein that translocates to the keratinocyte surface after ultraviolet exposure, where antibody-dependent cellular cytotoxicity produces the characteristic annular, polycyclic, photodistributed lesions of subacute cutaneous lupus erythematosus. The reaction spares the kidneys and central nervous system in typical cases, distinguishing it clinically from systemic drug-induced lupus, and it is characteristically reversible: lesions clear within weeks of withdrawing the offending drug, and recurrence after rechallenge has been documented. Reed et al. (PMID 3873891) reported five patients taking hydrochlorothiazide who developed photosensitive eruptions with the clinical and histologic features of subacute cutaneous lupus erythematosus and antibodies to the SS-A(Ro) antigen; the eruptions cleared after the drug was discontinued, anti-SS-A antibodies disappeared in one patient after thiazide withdrawal, and rechallenge with hydrochlorothiazide reproduced the dermatitis — the original human evidence, including the rechallenge that supports a causal rather than coincidental relationship. Lowe et al. (PMID 21039412) systematically reviewed drug-induced subacute cutaneous lupus erythematosus, noting that the initial appearance of SCLE lesions with Ro/SS-A autoantibodies as an adverse reaction to hydrochlorothiazide was first reported in 1985, that an increasing number of drug classes has since been implicated, and that most cases resolved within weeks of drug withdrawal with Ro/SS-A autoantibodies present in about 80 percent of cases where such data were available. Callen (PMID 20693204) reviews drug-induced subacute cutaneous lupus erythematosus and records that the first description dates to 1985, when a series of five patients was found to have hydrochlorothiazide-induced SCLE, and that at least 40 other drugs have since been implicated. Framing under 38 CFR § 3.310: this is a § 3.310(a) proximate-causation theory pleaded as a medication side effect, in which a disability caused by treatment of the service-connected hypertension is itself service-connected because the thiazide was prescribed for that service-connected condition. It is not a § 3.310(b) aggravation theory; aggravation would be the correct theory only where the record shows pre-existing cutaneous lupus or another photosensitive dermatosis and the claim is that the thiazide exposure measurably worsened a baseline skin disease, in which case the drug-attributable increment must be separated from the natural progression of that baseline dermatosis and § 3.310(b) governs. Chronology is decisive and the corresponding § 3.310(a) or (b) analysis requires: a prescription record identifying hydrochlorothiazide or a thiazide-containing product with start and stop dates; onset of the eruption after the drug was started, in a photodistributed pattern; dermatologic or histologic confirmation of an interface dermatitis compatible with SCLE and, where available, positive Ro/SS-A antibody testing; and documented improvement or resolution after the drug was withdrawn, since the natural history of resolution on withdrawal is itself strong evidence of the drug's causal role. Only then can an examiner state that the subacute cutaneous lupus erythematosus is at least as likely as not caused by the thiazide prescribed for the service-connected hypertension — a conclusion requiring documented chronology, accounted-for competing causes, and an approximate balance of evidence consistent with § 3.102. Original proposal mechanism (preserved verbatim):

The reaction spares the kidneys and central nervous system in typical cases, distinguishing it clinically from systemic drug-induced lupus, and it is characteristically reversible: lesions clear within weeks of withdrawing the offending drug, and recurrence after rechallenge has been documented. Reed et al. causalMechanism.primaryVector: Pharmacological iatrogenic sequence: statins inhibit 3-hydroxy-3-methylglutaryl-coenzyme A reductase, the rate-limiting enzyme of cholesterol synthesis. In genetically susceptible patients the drug upregulates expression of the HMGCR protein in regenerating skeletal muscle, and that overexpressed enzyme becomes the target of a specific autoantibody response, producing an immune-mediated necrotizing myopathy characterized by symmetric proximal muscle weakness, markedly elevated creatine kinase, myofiber necrosis with minimal inflammation on biopsy, and — critically — persistence and even progression after the statin is withdrawn, which distinguishes it from the self-limited toxic myopathy that resolves on discontinuation. Because the disease is antibody-driven rather than simply dose-toxic, the ordinary temporal assumption that stopping the drug ends the illness does not hold. Mammen et al. (PMID 21360500) identified anti-HMGCR autoantibodies in 45 of 750 patients presenting to a myositis center, with the great majority of patients aged 50 and older having had statin exposure, and demonstrated the statin-dependent upregulation of the autoantigen. Nazir et al. (PMID 28277343) systematically reviewed 100 reported cases of statin-associated autoimmune myopathy and described a syndrome of symmetric proximal weakness with extreme creatine kinase elevation, occurring predominantly in males, and separate from the ordinary statin myalgia that resolves on drug cessation. Khoo et al. (PMID 40347460) calculated the incidence of anti-HMGCR immune-mediated necrotizing myopathy across four independent cohorts in the United Kingdom and Australia and described its clinical characteristics, treating it as a rare but definable complication of statin therapy — the contemporary denominator evidence for a rare-event claim. Framing under 38 CFR § 3.310: this is a § 3.310(a) proximate-causation theory pleaded as a medication side effect, in which a disability caused by treatment of the service-connected hypertension is itself service-connected because the statin was prescribed for that service-connected condition. It is not a § 3.310(b) aggravation theory; aggravation would be the correct theory only where the record documents pre-existing myositis, inflammatory myopathy, or another myopathic process and the claim is that the statin exposure measurably worsened that baseline muscle disease, in which case the drug-attributable increment must be separated from the natural progression of the pre-existing myopathy and § 3.310(b) governs. Chronology and the individual analysis under § 3.310(a) or (b) require: a prescription record identifying the statin with start and stop dates and the indication of the service-connected hypertension or its cardiovascular risk profile; onset of proximal weakness during or after exposure; laboratory confirmation of markedly elevated creatine kinase; and, where available, positive anti-HMGCR antibody testing or muscle biopsy showing necrotizing myopathy, since the antibody and biopsy findings are what distinguish the immune-mediated disease from ordinary statin myalgia. Only then can an examiner state that the myositis is at least as likely as not caused by the statin prescribed for the service-connected hypertension — a conclusion requiring documented chronology, accounted-for competing causes, and an approximate balance of evidence consistent with § 3.102. Competing causes that must be excluded or weighed include ordinary statin-associated myalgia and self-limited toxic myopathy, hypothyroidism, vitamin D deficiency, inflammatory myopathies unrelated to statins (dermatomyositis, polymyositis, and other immune-mediated necrotizing myopathies), paraneoplastic myositis associated with an occult malignancy, viral myositis including influenza, HIV, and hepatitis, glucocorticoid or colchicine myopathy, alcohol-related muscle disease, and inherited metabolic myopathies. No individual probability is asserted here. No intentional rechallenge, unsupervised discontinuation of a prescribed statin, or patient-specific prescribing recommendation is made. Rating discipline under § 4.14: the same weakness, creatine kinase elevation, or limitation of motion may not be compensated more than once — a myositis rating under DC 5021 and a separate muscle-injury rating for the same proximal groups are not cumulative, and § 4.14 and the note to DCs 5013 through 5024 require a single evaluation for the same manifestation.
